summary:
Iraq is among the most dangerous countries in the world for a trans visitor. On 27 April 2024 the Council of Representatives passed an amendment to the 1988 Law on Combatting Prostitution that explicitly criminalises consensual same-sex relations, gender-affirming healthcare and diverse gender expression. The President signed the legislation on 29 June 2024 and it has been in force since 1 July 2024. The Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor, Human Rights Watch and ILGA Asia all record it as the operative legal baseline.

The penalties are severe. Consensual same-sex relations carry 10 to 15 years' imprisonment. Undergoing or performing a gender-affirming procedure carries 1 to 3 years, which places transition itself beyond the law. Country coverage also records penalties of up to 15 years together with fines and deportation, so removal from the country is a stated consequence of criminalised status. The statute separately penalises the promotion of homosexuality.

Iraq has no legal gender recognition framework, and the 2024 amendment closes the remaining gap. It criminalises biological sex changes undertaken on personal desire or inclination and punishes both the transgender person and the doctor; court-ordered procedures on intersex people are excluded. Legal sex-change documentation is therefore effectively unavailable.

Violence against LGBT Iraqis is long documented and largely unpunished. A BBC investigation found that dozens, possibly hundreds, of gay people have been killed in recent years while authorities turn a blind eye, and reports the UN assessment that state neglect makes Iraq a perpetrator rather than a protector. The US State Department's 2012 Human Rights Report for Iraq already documented societal discrimination and violence based on perceived sexual orientation and gender identity alongside sectarian violence, torture and impunity. On 27 October 2023 a prominent Iraqi TikToker was fatally shot in Baghdad amid a crackdown on the LGBTQ community.

Expression-based violence predates the current statute. In early 2012 a wave of killings targeted emo teenagers accused of homosexuality on the basis of their clothing, carried out by Shi'a death squads of the Mahdi Army; flyers appeared in Baghdad naming individuals and threatening them unless they cut their hair and abandoned non-conformist dress.

Marriage is closed to same-sex couples. Article 3 of the Iraqi Personal Status Law 1959 and Article 1 of the Iraqi Kurdistan Personal Status Law 1992 define marriage as a union between a man and a woman, and Article 7 requires couples seeking to marry to produce medical documents showing they are not infected with AIDS. The Personal Status Law was amended in 1981 to allow a wife to divorce her husband where he is guilty of a homosexual relationship, treated as infidelity.

Protection machinery is largely external and non-governmental. The UK Home Office's Country Policy and Information Note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Iraq (version 3.0, July 2025) assesses risk from state and hybrid actors and from non-state actors, together with protection, internal relocation and certification questions for LGBT+ asylum claims. Human Rights Watch called for outright repeal of the amendment on 20 May 2024, while the BBC recorded that supporters framed the law as upholding religious values and rights groups condemned it.
tangentialFactors:
The 2024 amendment sits inside a much older pattern of official tolerance for anti-LGBT violence rather than starting one. The US State Department recorded societal discrimination and violence based on perceived sexual orientation and gender identity in its 2012 Human Rights Report, more than a decade before the statute criminalised the conduct directly.

The escalation runs from the 2012 emo killings through the October 2023 shooting of a visible online figure to the 2024 legislation, with the BBC investigation into dozens, possibly hundreds, of killings and the UN finding of state neglect filling the years between. Impunity for the earlier violence is the constant across all three phases.

Human Rights Watch demanded outright repeal on 20 May 2024, while the BBC reported that the law's supporters presented it as upholding religious values and rights groups condemned it. The disagreement is over the existence of the offence, not its scope.

Under the former regime, after the disease reached Iraq in 1986, Saddam Hussein ordered all Iraqis with AIDS relocated to a special prison facility. Medical-status policing of this kind has a four-decade institutional history behind the 2024 medical-document and procedure provisions.

Adjacent jurisdictions in the region criminalise consensual same-sex conduct as well, but few couple that with an explicit ban on gender-affirming care imposed on both patient and physician and the absence of any recognition procedure, which is the combination a trans visitor to Iraq faces.
localsOnly:
Legal support and relocation for LGBT Iraqis are delivered overwhelmingly by NGOs. Iraqi LGBT, established September 2005, works on relocating LGBTQ people to safer countries, provides legal help for asylum seekers and maintains safe houses inside Iraq. The International Railroad for Queer Refugees, founded 2008, gives financial and resettlement assistance to LGBTQ asylum seekers fleeing persecution on sexual orientation or gender identity grounds.

OWFI led more than 40 local organisations to change Iraq's Anti-Shelter Policy, which had permitted only government-run shelters to exist. Rasan expanded its projects from 2016 as a partner of COC Nederland in the Pride Program, known locally as Crossing Iraqi Rainbow.

Iraqueer, formed in March 2015, runs education work including published guides on security and health safety, YouTube videos and workshops on gender and sexuality, and advocacy and safety support in crisis.

Residents also live under the personal-status provisions that visitors encounter only at the margin. Marriage is restricted to a man and a woman under Article 3 of the 1959 Iraqi Personal Status Law and Article 1 of the 1992 Iraqi Kurdistan Personal Status Law, couples must produce medical documents certifying the absence of AIDS under Article 7, and the 1981 amendment allows a wife to divorce a husband found guilty of a homosexual relationship treated as infidelity.

There is no route to legal gender recognition. The 2024 amendment punishes both the transgender person and the doctor for procedures undertaken on personal inclination, with court-ordered intersex interventions the sole exception, so identity documents cannot be brought into line with a person's gender.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two dates for the parliamentary passage appear in the sources, 27 April 2024 and 28 April 2024; the discrepancy is unresolved and the inventory does not explain it. The signature date of 29 June 2024 and the entry into force on 1 July 2024 are consistent across sources.

Whether the Kurdistan Regional Government applies the 2024 amendment within the Kurdistan Region, or relies on the 1992 Kurdistan Personal Status Law alone, is not addressed in the inventory and remains unresolved.

Reported sentences actually imposed under the new offences are not sourced here. The inventory gives statutory ranges of 10 to 15 years and 1 to 3 years, but no prosecution outcomes, and no figures for enforcement against trans defendants specifically.

Whether the fines and deportation consequence apply to every tier of the 2024 offence or only to some provisions is unclear from the sources. The same is true of the interaction between deportation and an asylum claim.

The personal-status provisions, the shelter-policy change and the NGO descriptions are drawn from encyclopaedic country coverage rather than primary legal texts or the organisations' own statements in this inventory, and have not been independently corroborated here.

The UK Home Office CPIN's specific findings on internal relocation options and on certification thresholds are summarised only at the level of topics covered; its detailed country-conditions assessment and its conclusions are not reproduced.
